title: Jude and the Language
premise: August Lockridge has spent eleven years writing postcards to the burned-down house on Vell Street, addressed to a sister who died in the fire — or so August believes. At their mother's funeral, a stranger named Jude recognizes the family by 'the Language,' a private code of gestures and invented words only the Lockridges ever shared, and claims to be the child August's sister smuggled out of the house that night. As August investigates Jude's story against every scrap of memory they own, they uncover evidence their mother started the fire to erase a secret — one Jude's existence threatens to expose. When the last postcard box is opened, August must choose between protecting the mother's legend and claiming the found family standing in front of them; they choose Jude, mailing one final postcard to an address that finally exists.
about_author: Sebastian Yarrow is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing undeliverable letters in a municipal dead-letter office. Their fiction explores the documents people leave behind when they cannot say things aloud, and this is their second novel.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: August's POV. We meet August at the dead-letter office where they work, then at home writing postcards to 14 Vell Street, a house that burned in 2013. The chapter establishes the ritual, the grief disguised as habit, and the practiced smile. Beat: loneliness mistaken for peace.

chapters.title: A Funeral in Good Weather
chapters.summary: August's POV. At their mother Marion's funeral, relatives offer platitudes while August performs composure. A young stranger lingers too long at the graveside, mouthing something with their hands — a gesture August hasn't seen since childhood. Beat: the past arriving uninvited.

chapters.title: The Word for Door
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude follows August from the cemetery and uses a Lockridge hand-sign for 'door' in the parking lot. They reveal they know the family's private language — invented by Marion and her daughters — and ask, simply, to talk. August walks away. Beat: terror dressed as refusal.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took
chapters.summary: August's POV. August revisits the official story: the 2013 fire killed their sister Wren; August was away at college. They dig out old photographs and find one of Marion holding a toddler no relative can name. Beat: the first crack in the sanctioned memory.

chapters.title: Coffee, Interrogated
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude and August finally meet at a diner. Jude tells their version: raised outside the family, taught the Language by Wren through years of letters, told to find the Lockridges only after Marion died. August dismantles every detail — except the ones they can't. Beat: wary gravity between two liars' inheritances.

chapters.title: The Postcard Box
chapters.summary: August's POV. August confesses their own secret — eleven years of postcards to a dead address — expecting ridicule. Instead Jude asks to read them. Reading aloud, August hears for the first time what they've actually been saying all these years. Beat: shame turning into recognition.

chapters.title: Duty, Illustrated
chapters.summary: August's POV. August's aunt Delphine warns them off Jude: the family settled everything after the fire, legally and otherwise, and reopening it serves no one. She hints that Marion paid someone to stay quiet. Beat: the machinery of family loyalty revealed as control.

chapters.title: Letters From a Burned House
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude shows August the letters Wren sent over fifteen years — postmarked from towns Wren supposedly never reached, written in the Language only the sisters knew. One letter mentions 'the thing Mother buried.' Beat: hope with teeth.

chapters.title: The Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: August's POV. August tracks down a retired firefighter from the Vell Street call. He remembers two people carried out that night, not one — and a third already gone before the trucks arrived. The report was amended. By whom, he won't say. Beat: the ground tilting.

chapters.title: Amended
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude admits they came not just for connection but for answers: Wren's letters promised proof of what happened, proof Jude needs to understand their own abandonment. August resents being needed as an archive rather than a sibling. Beat: love and use blurring dangerously.

chapters.title: Delphine's Ledger
chapters.summary: August's POV. Searching Marion's effects, August finds a ledger of payments to a man named Corliss spanning a decade after the fire. The final entry coincides with the amendment date. August realizes their mother bought the official story. Beat: grief curdling into betrayal.

chapters.title: The Middle of It
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. August brings the ledger to Jude; together they reconstruct the night — Wren escaping with a child, Marion choosing the house's secrets over her daughter. The chapter ends with August understanding why the postcards never felt finished. Beat: terrible clarity.

chapters.title: Corliss
chapters.summary: August's POV. August finds Corliss, now dying, in a care home. He confirms he altered the report for Marion but insists he never knew what she was covering up — only that she wept while paying him. Beat: a villain revealed as another mourner.

chapters.title: What Wren Buried
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Following a clue in Wren's last letter, Jude and August return to the ruins of 14 Vell Street, now a vacant lot. In the foundation's edge they find a weatherproof tin: Wren's journal and a photograph of Marion, pregnant, years before August was born. Beat: the secret surfacing.

chapters.title: The First Daughter
chapters.summary: August's POV. The journal reveals Marion had a first daughter, Iris, given away in shame decades earlier — and that Wren discovered it, threatening to tell. The fire wasn't erasure of a stranger's secret; it was Marion burning her own history, with Wren inside it by accident. Beat: horror without a villain to hold.

chapters.title: Running Out of Time
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude falls ill — a chronic condition they'd hidden, the real reason they sought family before it was too late. In the hospital, Jude asks August not for truth anymore but for presence. August, terrified of losing another sibling, retreats to old habits. Beat: fear repeating its oldest mistake.

chapters.title: The Unsent
chapters.summary: August's POV. Alone with the postcard box, August writes a card to Wren admitting everything: that they chose the comfortable story, that they almost walked away from Jude the way the family walked away from Iris. They don't mail it. Beat: confession as rehearsal for change.

chapters.title: Forgiving the Photograph
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. August returns to the hospital and reads Wren's letters aloud to Jude, finishing the correspondence Wren began — becoming the link in the chain instead of its broken end. They forgive the stranger in the photographs: Marion, Wren, themselves. Beat: grace earned, not granted.

chapters.title: Delphine Comes Calling
chapters.summary: August's POV. Delphine arrives with lawyers and an ultimatum: recant publicly or be cut off, as Iris was. August realizes the family's duty has always been a blade pointed inward. They refuse — and are disowned in a kitchen that smells like every childhood Christmas. Beat: the cost made flesh.

chapters.title: The Last Address
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Recovering, Jude gives August a gift: a forwarding address — Jude's own apartment — and asks August to keep writing postcards, but somewhere mail can actually arrive. August mails the first one that evening: a single word in the Language meaning 'home.' Beat: ritual transformed.

chapters.title: Iris
chapters.summary: August's POV. Using the journal, August finds Iris — elderly, living two towns over, alive. The meeting is quiet and imperfect; Iris wants no reckoning, only tea. But she teaches August one sign neither Wren nor Jude knew, completing the Language. Beat: reconciliation without resolution.

chapters.title: Postscript, With Stamp
chapters.summary: August's POV, epistolary fragments throughout. Months later: August's desk holds incoming mail now, not just outgoing — cards from Jude, a note from Iris, even one unsigned from Delphine. The final image is August at 14 Vell Street's lot, planting something, then walking home to answer a letter. Beat: arrival, ongoing.
